organism: Rubella virus, the sole member of the genus Rubivirus (family Matonaviridae): an enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus with a single antigenic type.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period averages 14 days (range 12-23). Up to 50% of infections are subclinical. In young children, rash is often the first symptom; older children and adults may have a 1-5 day prodrome of low-grade fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, and upper respiratory symptoms first. The maculopapular rash appears 14-17 days after exposure, starts on the face, progresses head to foot, and lasts about 3 days - it is fainter than a measles rash and does not coalesce. Postauricular, posterior cervical, and suboccipital lymphadenopathy is characteristic. Arthralgia and arthritis are rare in children and men but common in adult women, sometimes lasting up to a month. Serious complications are rare: hemorrhagic manifestations (about 1 in 3,000 cases, most often thrombocytopenic purpura) and encephalitis (about 1 in 6,000 cases, occasionally fatal).
epidemiologySummary: Rubella is a human-only disease with no known animal reservoir or insect transmission. It spreads via direct contact or respiratory droplets, including from subclinical or asymptomatic cases (up to 50% of all infections). Since US elimination, cases occur with no temporal pattern, typically imported or linked to an imported case. A case is considered contagious from 7 days before through 7 days after rash onset; infants with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) can shed large quantities of virus for up to a year.
secularTrendsSummary: Rubella and CRS became nationally notifiable in 1966. Incidence declined dramatically after vaccine introduction in 1969. Postvaccine outbreaks among adolescents and young adults and in unvaccinated-adult settings led to recommendations to vaccinate susceptible postpubertal women, military personnel, college students, and workers in certain settings. Endemic rubella was declared eliminated in the US in 2004 (fewer than 10 cases and less than 1 CRS case per year), and since 2012 every US rubella case has been import-associated.
vaccineDescription: The first rubella vaccines were licensed in 1969; the current vaccine strain, RA 27/3, was licensed in 1979. There is no single-antigen rubella vaccine available in the US - rubella protection comes only via MMR (MMR-II) or MMRV (ProQuad). Both are live, attenuated, lyophilized, reconstituted with sterile water, given subcutaneously, and contain gelatin and neomycin with no adjuvant or preservative.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Routine schedule is 2 doses of MMR: dose 1 at 12-15 months (minimum age 12 months), dose 2 at 4-6 years, with a minimum interval of 4 weeks (3 months for MMRV, though 4 weeks is still valid). As with measles and mumps, separate MMR and varicella vaccines are generally preferred over MMRV for the first dose in children 12-47 months because of a higher febrile-seizure risk with MMRV at that age.
evidenceOfImmunitySummary: A person can generally be considered immune to rubella if born before 1957, has serologic evidence of immunity (an equivocal result counts as negative), has laboratory-confirmed disease, or has documentation of adequate vaccination. Unlike measles and mumps, birth before 1957 is explicitly NOT acceptable evidence of rubella immunity for women who could become pregnant - it is only presumptive. Clinical diagnosis of rubella is considered too unreliable to use at all in assessing immune status, since many rash illnesses mimic it and many infections go unrecognized; the only reliable evidence of past infection is serum rubella IgG from a laboratory that regularly performs the test.
vaccineEfficacySummary: At least 95% of people vaccinated at 12 months or older develop serologic evidence of immunity after a single dose, and more than 90% retain protection against clinical rubella for at least 15 years; a single dose appears to confer long-term, probably lifelong protection. Although antibody titers wane over the years, there is no evidence this leads to meaningful susceptibility to clinical rubella or CRS - both remain extremely rare among vaccinated people in the US.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication, as is severe immunocompromise (malignancy, chemotherapy, congenital immunodeficiency, long-term immunosuppressive therapy, or HIV with severe immunosuppression), high-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy for 14 or more days (wait at least 1 month after stopping), a family history of congenital or hereditary immunodeficiency in a first-degree relative (unless the recipient's own immunocompetence is verified), and pregnancy. MMRV additionally treats HIV infection, regardless of immune status, as a contraindication. Precautions include moderate/severe acute illness, alpha-gal allergy, recent receipt of antibody-containing blood products (wait 3-11 months), a history of thrombocytopenic purpura, and an upcoming TB skin test. Egg allergy is not a reason for special precautions.
vaccineSafetySummary: Because rubella protection is delivered only via MMR or MMRV, the general safety profile matches the Measles chapter's (fever, transient rash, febrile seizures, rare anaphylaxis). Distinctively for rubella: arthralgia and other joint symptoms, attributed to the rubella component, occur in up to 25% of adult women.
vaccineStorageSummary: Follow manufacturer guidance for MMR-II and ProQuad specifically; see CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for general best practices.
surveillanceSummary: Because clinical diagnosis is unreliable, laboratory confirmation relies on PCR detection of rubella virus, a significant IgG rise between acute and convalescent sera, or rubella-specific IgM (optimal collection is at least 5 days after symptom onset; retest if an earlier sample is IgM-negative). Suspected CRS in infants should be evaluated with nasopharyngeal and/or urine testing as close to birth as possible, with monthly viral-shedding screens after age 3 months until two consecutive negative results, since shedding can persist up to a year. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS)
supplementalTopics.summary: Preventing CRS is the central objective of rubella vaccination programs. Maternal infection is most damaging in early gestation - risk is highest when rubella is acquired in the first 12 weeks - and can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or birth defects including deafness, eye abnormalities (cataracts, glaucoma, retinopathy, microphthalmia), and congenital heart disease. Infants with CRS can shed large quantities of virus for up to a year and may transmit rubella to susceptible caregivers.

supplementalTopics.title: Reducing Susceptibility in Women of Childbearing Age
supplementalTopics.summary: Because presumptive immunity from birth before 1957 is not accepted for women who could become pregnant, elimination-maintenance efforts specifically target vaccinating susceptible adolescents and women of childbearing age - especially those born outside the US - through family planning and STD clinics, routine gynecologic care, follow-up on premarital serology results, college vaccination requirements, postpartum and postabortion vaccination, and workplaces employing people born outside the US.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination in Pregnancy
supplementalTopics.summary: Pregnancy is a contraindication to MMR/MMRV, and pregnancy should be avoided for 4 weeks after vaccination - but inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy is not a reason to consider ending it. A study of 321 susceptible vaccinated women found no CRS among their offspring; multi-country follow-up of 1,980 susceptible pregnant women found congenital rubella infection in 3.6% of infants but no cases with CRS-associated birth defects.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination of Adults and Healthcare Personnel
supplementalTopics.summary: Adults born in 1957 or later need at least 1 documented MMR dose or other acceptable evidence of immunity. Students entering college or other post-high-school institutions should have 2 documented doses. Health care personnel need 2 doses for measles/mumps immunity and 1 dose for rubella immunity - including those born before 1957 - and facilities should offer an additional outbreak-specific dose to personnel during a measles or mumps outbreak (2 doses) or rubella outbreak (1 dose).

keyPoints: First described as a disease distinct from measles/scarlet fever in 1814 (hence 'German measles')
Congenital rubella syndrome was first recognized in 1941 by an Australian ophthalmologist investigating congenital cataracts after a 1940 rubella epidemic
No single-antigen rubella vaccine exists in the US; rubella protection comes only via MMR or MMRV
Endemic rubella was declared eliminated in the US in 2004; since 2012 all US cases have been import-associated
Birth before 1957 is NOT acceptable evidence of rubella immunity for women who could become pregnant, unlike the more permissive rule for measles and mumps
Clinical diagnosis of rubella is too unreliable to assess immune status - only laboratory-confirmed serum IgG counts
Arthralgia after MMR vaccination, tied to the rubella component, affects up to 25% of adult women
